title: PostgreSQL-class primary failure
description: Walk a primary crash from detection through fencing, promotion, retries, and user-visible UNKNOWN. This path is not instantaneous, lossless, or transparent.
assumptions: One writable PostgreSQL primary, one or more streaming replicas, WAL on disk, application connection pool.

synchronous_commit is on for the primary's local flush; replica apply on this walkthrough is asynchronous unless a step says otherwise. Acknowledged commits can still be missing on the promoted replica. That RPO>0 story is not RDS Multi-AZ (managed synchronous standby + DNS/CNAME cutover).

A membership/fencing service (Patroni/etcd-class, STONITH, or equivalent) is allowed to revoke the writer lease. Client timeouts alone do not authorize promotion. Managed sync-standby products still need fencing and UNKNOWN handling; they are not an async-loss path.
Clients retry writes only with idempotency keys. Timeouts are UNKNOWN, not rollback.
Observability is derived. Missing metrics do not prove a commit was lost or succeeded.

steps.title: Healthy primary
steps.timeline: t0: primary holds the writer lease/epoch. WAL flushes locally. Replicas apply behind by measured lag (example: 40–200 ms under 15 MB/s WAL).
steps.inFlight: In-flight commits wait on WAL fsync and client round trip. Pool connections are checked out.
steps.consistency: Primary reads under default READ COMMITTED see a per-statement snapshot, not session snapshot isolation. Replica reads may miss the last commit unless the client carries a {timeline, LSN} token and waits.
steps.durability: A commit the primary acknowledged is on the primary's WAL. It is on a replica only if that replica flushed that LSN.
steps.userVisible: p99 is pool wait + SQL + fsync. No failover UX.
steps.recovery: Not in this step. Keep lag and lease metrics on a dashboard; they are detection inputs later.

steps.title: Detect loss of writer
steps.timeline: t1: primary process, disk, or network dies. Lease renewals stop. Health checks fail after the configured interval (often seconds, not milliseconds).
steps.inFlight: Clients blocked on the dead primary hit timeouts. The server may have flushed WAL without sending the Ready response.
steps.consistency: There is no current proven writer. Replica state is whatever LSN they flushed. Do not read 'the old hostname' as authority.
steps.durability: Unknown for in-flight statements. Already-acked commits exist on the old primary's disk if the disk is intact, and on replicas that received them.
steps.userVisible: Errors, spinner timeouts, HTTP 504/UNKNOWN. Not a clean 409.
steps.recovery: Do not promote on a single probe. Require lease expiry plus replica data comparison. DNS/VIP still pointing at the corpse is expected for TTL seconds.

steps.title: In-flight commit impact
steps.timeline: t1–t2: statements that were in WAL-flush or in the TCP response path have no client-visible outcome.
steps.inFlight: Three classes: (1) never reached WAL, (2) WAL flushed, client not told, (3) client told OK but replica never got the record.
steps.consistency: Two clients can now disagree: one saw timeout, one saw OK if it completed earlier. Session state on the app is not a source of truth.
steps.durability: Class (2) is durable on the old primary and maybe not on the promotion candidate. Class (3) is durable on the old primary; promotion can drop it if that replica was behind.
steps.userVisible: Retries without idempotency double-apply class (2)/(3) if the new primary has the row, or create a second row if it does not.
steps.recovery: Treat timeout as UNKNOWN. Look up the idempotency key on the new primary after promotion. Do not auto-replay unsigned request logs.

steps.title: Fence and promote
steps.timeline: t2: coordinator fences the old writer (revoke lease, block writes at storage/VIP, increment epoch). Then it promotes the replica with the latest eligible flushed WAL.
steps.inFlight: Old primary, if it heals, must be rejected: fenced epoch, STONITH, or rewind. Unfenced heal is split-brain.
steps.consistency: After promotion, the new timeline is not an ancestor of unreplicated old-primary WAL. Do not compare LSN numbers across timelines; carry {timeline, LSN}.
steps.durability: Any WAL only on the fenced primary and not on the promotee is unreadable unless you rewind/merge by hand. That is data loss relative to a client who heard OK.
steps.userVisible: A window of errors while VIP/DNS/pool move. Connection reset, not a seamless swap.
steps.recovery: Write a no-op or timeline history on the new primary. Routers must require the new epoch. Do not claim the cutover was lossless.

steps.title: Client retries
steps.timeline: t3: app retries with the same idempotency key after backoff. Pool reconnects to the new writer.
steps.inFlight: If the original commit is on the new primary, the unique key hits and returns the prior result. If it is not, the retry commits a new authoritative row.
steps.consistency: Read-your-writes tokens must include timeline/epoch. A retry that lands on a lagging replica can miss the new commit.
steps.durability: The retry is durable only when the new primary acknowledges under the current fsync policy.
steps.userVisible: User may see success on retry, duplicate side effects if the key was missing, or a second timeout.
steps.recovery: Idempotency store on the primary with UNIQUE (tenant, operation, key). At-least-once clients plus uniqueness, not exactly-once networking.

steps.title: Consistency after cutover
steps.timeline: t3–t4: replicas that were behind the promotee must rewind or rebuild. Caches still hold pre-failover values.
steps.inFlight: Cache-aside hits can return rows the new timeline never had, or miss rows it just committed.
steps.consistency: Session monotonicity is broken across timelines. Linearizable reads require proving current authority (lease/ReadIndex), not 'hostname role=primary'.
steps.durability: Caches and search indexes are derived; rebuilding them does not restore lost WAL.
steps.userVisible: Stale profile reads, missing 'success' records, or brief duplicates in derived views.
steps.recovery: Invalidate or version-bump cache keys. Search reindex from the new primary. Do not LWW TokenX balances from a replica.

steps.title: Restore redundancy
steps.timeline: t4–t5: attach a new replica, restore sync durability targets, confirm backups include the new timeline.
steps.inFlight: Catch-up generates WAL apply load. Routing correctness-sensitive reads to a catching replica is unsafe.
steps.consistency: Until a second copy exists, a second crash is a longer outage and a worse RPO.
steps.durability: RPO is 'last WAL on the current primary' until another replica or archive acknowledges.
steps.userVisible: Degraded SLO: higher p99 while catch-up and vacuum/checkpoint catch the new writer.
steps.recovery: Seed from snapshot+WAL, never from unsigned request logs. Fence any node still on the old timeline.

steps.title: What users should be told
steps.timeline: Whole incident RTO: detection delay + fence + promote + pool/DNS reconnect is typically seconds to minutes, not a single RTT. RPO is separate: last WAL on the promotee vs an ACK the old primary already sent.
steps.inFlight: Some users saw success, some saw error, some saw retry success. Support must not promise all three match.
steps.consistency: After recovery, the ledger is the new primary. Disputes are UNKNOWN until the idempotency row is read there.
steps.durability: If a user got OK and that WAL was only on the fenced disk, the honest answer is possible acknowledged loss under async replica policy.
steps.userVisible: Status page: writes paused, elevated errors, some requests uncertain. Do not tell customers the cutover hid all loss.
steps.recovery: Reconcile UNKNOWN with the idempotency table and customer receipts. Compensation is a business transaction, not a silent overwrite.
